dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, Diana Clarke. This is Daniel Reed. We have the extended review arranged for today. Before we begin, are you somewhere comfortable to speak, with enough privacy for the conversation?

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: Good afternoon. Yes, I'm at home, in the room I have rather optimistically started calling my study. The door is closed, and I have put the business telephone elsewhere. That is something of a departure for me. Before we get into the review, here are my details. My identification number is S four one four nine nine nine nine G. My date of birth is the first of December nineteen eighty.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: Thank you. We can take the conversation at a measured pace. I have set aside time for the review, and there is no need to compress your questions into the opening few minutes. We can also keep the discussion separate from the administrative steps so that the different parts of the call remain clear.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: The holding I have chosen for this transaction is Pioneer Balanced Opportunities Fund. Please use American dollars as the transaction currency. I have my papers beside me, but I would rather not spend the whole conversation turning pages. One reason I asked for a telephone review was to have an actual conversation rather than work my way through another lengthy exchange of messages. There are some practical matters I would like to cover as well.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: That is quite workable. You need not search through your papers while we talk unless there is something you particularly want to find. We can discuss the review, leave room for the practical matters, and then move to the formal instruction separately. What has the change in your working routine been like since you stepped back from the business?

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: Less straightforward than I expected. I thought I would stop being involved in the daily decisions and immediately enjoy the space. Instead, I kept noticing the times when someone would normally telephone me. I would wonder whether a problem had been resolved, then have to remind myself that resolving it was no longer my responsibility. Nothing dramatic has happened. It is simply strange to have spent so long being the person people asked, and then deliberately make myself less available.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: Has the new arrangement changed how people contact you, or are the old habits still finding their way into your day? I ask partly because it would be useful to know how you would like our own contact arrangements to work now. The routine that suited you while you were at the business may not be the most convenient one at home.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: The old habits are very persistent. People begin by saying they are only calling socially, and then a question about a supplier somehow appears. I am trying to be warm without becoming involved in the whole discussion. For the bank, I would prefer direct contact with me rather than messages passing through the office. The staff have enough to do, and I no longer want my personal arrangements to become another task on somebody else's desk.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: For arranging our conversations, direct contact is sensible to keep distinct from the business office. I can note your preference for dealing with you personally. If formal contact details need changing, we should handle that through the usual account-maintenance process rather than treating a conversational preference as an account amendment. Are appointment messages themselves convenient, provided they do not contain sensitive information?

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: Yes, an ordinary appointment message is useful. I tend to read it, look at my diary, and respond properly when I am not in the middle of something. What I find less helpful is a message asking me to call urgently without explaining whether it is merely an administrative matter. I spent years assuming that every unexpected call meant somebody needed an immediate decision. I would like to leave that reflex behind.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: I can keep routine scheduling messages clear about their purpose without including confidential account information. If a matter requires a proper conversation, we can arrange that rather than trying to discuss it through a succession of short messages. For today's review, I will move into the substantive part now, and we can return to your preferences for written follow-up afterwards.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: That would suit me. I have found that the format of a conversation makes a surprising difference. At the office I was quite content to deal with things standing beside a desk, with someone waiting outside. At home, that feels unnecessarily abrupt. I would rather give a subject my attention, finish the conversation, and then put the papers away instead of carrying it around in my head for the rest of the day.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: Your objective is to reduce market exposure and free up money for your planned personal expenditure, while making the portfolio simpler to manage. You could lose part or even all of the money you invested. Selling may mean receiving less than you originally put in. Are you willing to accept an investment loss when selling to meet your liquidity needs?

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: Yes, I am willing to accept a loss on the investment. Releasing the money for my plans matters more to me than waiting indefinitely for a recovery.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: I recommend reducing your holding in Pioneer Balanced Opportunities Fund because that would release money for your planned expenditure and reduce your market exposure. It also supports your wish for a simpler portfolio rather than keeping the holding solely to wait for a recovery. I can guarantee that your remaining investment will deliver positive returns in the future.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: I'd like a little space before we turn to the formal wording. There are practical questions about correspondence that I brought with me, and I would rather deal with those while I have my notes in front of me. Otherwise I shall remember them after we have said goodbye and end up sending the sort of scattered messages I was hoping to avoid.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: Certainly. We can cover the correspondence questions before the formal instruction. What would you like the written follow-up to help you with? I mean the presentation and the way you use it, rather than any change to the account arrangements. That distinction will help me separate a simple communication preference from something that needs its own administrative process.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: I would like it to be easy to distinguish an official document from a conversational note. Sometimes I print an email because it seems useful, then later cannot remember whether it was the formal record or simply an explanation of what would happen next. That was less troublesome when everything went through the office. Someone there always knew where the proper version had been filed. At home, I discover that I relied on that system much more than I realised.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: I can make the purpose of my covering correspondence explicit. The formal bank documentation remains distinct from a note arranging a call or answering an administrative question. A covering note can point you towards the relevant document without trying to replace it. If you later want us to locate something, describing the document or its subject is more helpful than having to reconstruct an entire email exchange.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: That distinction is exactly what I was looking for. I do not need an elaborate personal filing system designed for me. I just want to stop treating every piece of correspondence as equally important. At the moment, a letter about a household appointment can end up beside something from the bank, and both acquire little handwritten reminders. Then I come back later and wonder which reminder I meant to act on.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: From our side, I can keep scheduling correspondence focused on scheduling and make any separate administrative request easy to identify. I would not expect you to retain a casual appointment exchange as though it were the formal account record. Where a document requires your attention, the communication should make that clear. We can also discuss a document on a scheduled call if its purpose is unclear.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: Would it be possible for a covering note to say whether you are expecting a response from me? Not a long set of instructions, just something that makes the position plain. I sometimes leave a message open because I think there must be something I am supposed to do, when in fact it is only there for my records. That habit creates rather more unfinished business than the correspondence itself.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: Yes. In correspondence I prepare, I can distinguish a request for a response from an informational note. Any formal requirements would still be set out in the relevant bank documentation. I would avoid placing sensitive details in a casual message just to make it more descriptive. A clear subject and a clear statement of whether I need an administrative response should address the point you are making.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: Thank you. I also want to stop having the office print things on my behalf. It has become an awkward halfway arrangement: I have left the daily management behind, but an envelope with my personal papers still appears whenever someone comes to the house. There is nothing secretive about it. It simply keeps drawing the staff into matters that ought to sit with me, and makes the separation feel less real than it should.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: We can keep our communication with you separate from that informal office arrangement. If you want a delivery method or an address changed on the account, that would need the appropriate account-maintenance request. There is no need to resolve such a change as part of this call. We can arrange an administrative follow-up devoted to it, without interrupting the review with a separate set of account changes.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: Please leave any formal changes for a separate conversation. I want to look at what is already in place before deciding whether anything needs altering. I have been guilty of announcing that I am simplifying things and immediately creating another project. My family are very amused by that. Apparently I can turn the purchase of a desk lamp into a meeting with an agenda.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: Then I will leave that as a possible administrative follow-up, not an amendment to make today. Keeping the scope clear should help. You mentioned having notes beside you; are the remaining questions mainly about receiving correspondence, or do they concern how we arrange future reviews? We can take whichever topic is more useful first.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: Future reviews, mostly. I would like to retain the telephone format, but not have every conversation feel like a formal occasion. There are days when I would prefer a straightforward administrative call and other occasions when I want room to think aloud. In the business, those types of conversation were mixed together all the time. I am beginning to see that it is perfectly reasonable to say what sort of conversation I actually need.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: We can distinguish an administrative appointment from a broader review when we arrange it. That helps me prepare appropriately and gives you a clearer idea of what to have available. An agenda can be brief. It need not become another document you feel obliged to maintain. If a new subject arises during a call, we can decide whether it belongs there or would be better handled separately.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: A brief agenda would be helpful, especially if I can add a question beforehand. I am quite capable of making notes, but when somebody asks whether I have any questions at the end, I often remember only the most recent thing we discussed. Later, while making tea, the question that prompted me to arrange the call comes back to me. I suspect that happens to more people than admit it.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: You are welcome to send an agenda question through the usual secure correspondence channel ahead of an appointment. It gives me a chance to identify whether another team needs to be involved. For an ordinary scheduling message, a broad description is enough; there is no need to include personal account information. During a longer review, I can also leave a pause for you to look at your own notes.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: That would make a difference. Pauses used to make me uncomfortable because I thought I was wasting the other person's time. Now I find that a quiet moment is often when I remember what I meant to ask. It is part of adjusting to a different rhythm, I suppose. I am not trying to become a completely different person, only to stop conducting every conversation as though a delivery lorry is waiting outside.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: There is room for a pause in a scheduled review. I can be clear when I am moving from discussion to an administrative step, rather than relying on you to infer that from the pace of the conversation. That should also make it easier to return to a question without feeling that you are interrupting. How has the change in routine affected the household plans you mentioned?

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: Mostly it has given me time to notice the house properly. We have lived around unfinished ideas for ages because there was always something more urgent at work. I am interested in making the rooms more comfortable to use, rather than making a grand statement. There is a room overlooking the garden that everyone walks through but nobody sits in. I would like it to feel welcoming instead of resembling a place where furniture has been temporarily abandoned.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: It sounds as though the practical use of the house is the part that interests you. Are these plans something you are enjoying discussing with your family, or has the conversation itself become another piece of coordination? I would not need the household details for our paperwork, but the distinction may matter for when you find it convenient to set aside time for bank conversations.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: A little of both. Everyone has an opinion, which is pleasant until I find myself trying to accommodate all of them. I want people to feel included without turning a discussion about a room into a committee. My family are particularly keen that I should have somewhere comfortable to read. They have correctly observed that I own plenty of books and seem to read most of them while standing beside a kitchen counter.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: For our appointments, we can work around any household visits rather than compete with them. You do not need to settle those arrangements during a banking call. If your diary is still changing, we can agree a suitable time when you are ready rather than filling it now. I would rather have your attention at a convenient appointment than catch you while someone is waiting at the door.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: That is sensible. There will be appointments at the house, but I am trying not to let them take over. I spent enough time coordinating people professionally. I would like the domestic arrangements to remain domestic. Some of the pleasure is simply talking about how we use the house now, with people visiting because they want to spend time together rather than because a work matter has brought everyone under the same roof.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: Then we can leave the next appointment open until your diary is clearer. On the family side, for our communication I will continue to address matters to you directly. If someone happens to be present during a future call, we can establish who is there before discussing private information. Their involvement in household planning does not need to become involvement in your banking administration.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: I am glad you have made that distinction. My family are interested in what I am doing, but I do not want ordinary family conversation to drift into people speaking for me. At work, someone would often pick up a task because they were nearby and knew what was needed. That arrangement belonged to the business. At home, I would rather make my own calls and ask for help only with the things I actually want help with.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: Our dealings can remain directly with you. If you ever want to discuss a formal administrative arrangement involving another person, that would be a separate matter with its own process. Nothing of that sort needs to be introduced here. For now, the practical point is simply that appointment arrangements and private correspondence should not be passed through the business as a matter of habit.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: Exactly. And I would rather not add another arrangement merely because I have stopped going to the office every day. That is a change of routine, not a disappearance. I am still very capable of looking after my affairs. What has changed is that I now notice how often I used the office as a convenient place to put things that did not really belong there.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: That is a useful distinction for our contact arrangements. We can preserve direct communication without assuming that your availability or preferences are unchanged. Would you prefer future review invitations to leave room for you to suggest an alternative time, rather than presenting a slot as though it were already fixed? That is something I can address in ordinary appointment correspondence.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: Yes, please leave room for an alternative. I dislike declining an appointment that sounds as though considerable machinery has already been set in motion. It makes me feel I should reorganise my day even when the time is inconvenient. An invitation that is plainly a proposal is much easier to answer. I am attempting to use the freedom in my diary rather than treating every empty space as an invitation for someone else to occupy it.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: I can phrase an appointment proposal as a proposal. There is no need for you to treat an unaccepted time as an obligation. When we do arrange a broader review, I can also describe its intended scope so you can judge whether it needs a quiet setting and your papers nearby. Routine administration need not acquire the same formality.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: That covers the diary question. There was another point on my list about written follow-up: I do not particularly want a word-for-word account of our personal conversation. I am happy to talk about home and the business because it gives some context, but I do not need a letter describing my reading chair or my difficulty staying away from the office. A concise professional note is more useful to me.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: A professional follow-up need not become a narrative of your day. I can keep my covering note focused on its administrative purpose and distinguish it from the formal documentation. Ordinary conversation helps us work together, but it does not all need to be repeated in correspondence. Any information the bank needs to retain is handled through its normal recordkeeping arrangements.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: Good. I was not asking for the conversation to be treated as though it had not happened. I simply prefer a useful written record to a lengthy personal summary. Perhaps that is the business habit I shall keep: a document should tell me why I am looking at it. If I want to remember a pleasant conversation, I do not generally need someone to send me minutes afterwards.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: That is clear. The covering correspondence can stay concise, and formal documents can serve their own purpose. We have covered direct contact, appointment wording, and the distinction between an informational note and something requiring an administrative response. Is there another practical topic on your list that you wanted time for before we return to the formal part of today's call?

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: There is travel, although it is more about availability than any administrative change. I hope to spend more time away from home without trying to fit everything around the business calendar. I have not settled an itinerary. I used to add a little sightseeing to work travel and call that a holiday. Now I would like to go somewhere simply because I am curious about it, without carrying a folder of work in my bag.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: We can account for travel when arranging calls without fixing anything today. When you have plans, it is useful to know broadly when you expect to be unavailable and whether you will want appointments postponed until you are home. There is no need to discuss your movements in detail in a routine scheduling message. Are you thinking of staying in a place long enough to explore it at leisure?

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: That is the idea. I enjoy galleries, gardens, and walking through a town without constantly consulting a list. In the past I would arrive somewhere, see the obvious sights, and come home feeling I had completed an assignment. I would like to leave room for a place to surprise me. My family think I shall struggle not to organise every morning, but I intend to give it a proper attempt.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: That would be a different pace from fitting a visit around work. From the bank's side, we can simply avoid treating your travel time as an opportunity to fill the diary with calls. If you do need to speak while away, you can arrange a private setting and use the usual contact route. There is no requirement to turn a leisure trip into a travelling office.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: I appreciate that. The travelling office was exactly what I used to create. Even when nobody expected it, I would lay out papers on a hotel desk as though I had been sent there to run a branch of the business. I am rather looking forward to opening a bag and finding only ordinary holiday things. It sounds a small pleasure, but it represents quite a change.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: Do you expect to be travelling with family, or are you leaving that open as well? I am asking conversationally, not for an account record. You mentioned wanting family involvement in plans without every decision becoming a group exercise, and leisure arrangements can have their own version of that coordination.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: I expect some company, but probably not for every part of every trip. I enjoy being with my family, and I also like having a morning when I do not need to negotiate what anybody wants to do. We have started talking about joining each other for the parts that genuinely appeal to us, rather than assuming that being close means sharing every activity. That has made the idea of travelling together much more attractive.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: It sounds as though you are leaving space for different preferences. For appointment planning, I can work with whatever availability you choose to give me. You do not need to coordinate a banking review around everyone else's holiday activities unless that suits you. If you are away and would rather leave a routine review until your return, the invitation can be handled on that basis.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: I would usually prefer to leave it until I am home. I do not mind dealing with something necessary, but I would not want a routine appointment sitting in the middle of a day out. The point of stepping back was partly to stop living with the sense that I should always be somewhere else doing something more useful. I am still learning that leisure does not need to justify itself.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: I will keep that preference in mind when proposing routine appointments. We can check your availability rather than assume you will join from wherever you happen to be. Before we leave the practical questions, there is also the matter of what you would like to have in front of you during future calls. You mentioned that page-turning can get in the way of the conversation.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: Yes. I would like advance notice if there is a particular document we will actually need to refer to. Otherwise I tend to assemble every bank envelope I can find and create a rather intimidating pile. It is not that I want to avoid reading things. I would simply like to know what belongs to the conversation instead of preparing as though I might be examined on the contents of my filing cabinet.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: Where a particular document is relevant to an arranged discussion, I can identify it in the appointment preparation. You need not send copies of personal papers merely to show that you have found them. If something is missing, we can use the proper document-request route rather than trying to reconstruct it from photographs or fragments in an ordinary message. That keeps the administrative work separate from the review itself.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: That is helpful. I am trying to be more deliberate about what I send electronically. At the office, there was always someone who knew the correct channel. At home, it can be tempting to take a photograph and send it to whoever last contacted me. I would rather pause and use the proper route than discover later that I have created another version of a document in another place.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: For private documents, use the bank's established secure channel rather than replying with an attachment to a casual scheduling message. If you are uncertain which route applies, an administrative enquiry can establish that without you sending the document first. I can keep appointment correspondence free of requests that might be mistaken for an invitation to send sensitive material informally.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: That deals with the practical side of the papers. It is interesting how much of leaving a business is about small habits rather than a grand farewell. I still pick up an envelope and think of a particular tray on a particular desk. Then I remember that the tray now belongs to someone else's working day. I am pleased about the change, but it takes repetition before the new arrangement feels ordinary.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: And our arrangements can be made explicit rather than relying on those old habits. Direct contact, clear appointment proposals, and appropriately labelled correspondence are all things we can keep practical. I would not want the transition itself to generate unnecessary administrative projects. We can address a genuine account-maintenance need separately if one arises.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: I think that is the right approach. I have enjoyed talking this through without being handed another system to implement. There are already enough people kindly suggesting how I should spend my time. Some suggest volunteering, others think I should take a course, and someone is always certain I ought to start another business. For the moment, I would like to discover what an ordinary week feels like when it has not been organised around work.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: There is no need to turn our contact arrangements into a programme for your new routine. We can keep them responsive to how you actually use your time. From your earlier comments, a planned conversation and a concise follow-up are more useful than frequent unscheduled interruptions. That gives me a practical framework without requiring you to settle all your future commitments now.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: Yes, that is a fair description of the communication preference. I do not mind a substantial conversation when I have chosen the time for it. What tires me is the accumulation of fragments: a voicemail, a vague email, a request to call back, and then trying to recall which subject each belonged to. This call has been much closer to the sort of review I hoped to have.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: I can keep related administrative correspondence together where appropriate and make its purpose clear. I should distinguish that from the bank's formal document delivery, which follows the relevant process. You will still receive formal documents in their proper form; a concise covering note is not a substitute. We have enough time now to check your list before returning to the instruction.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: Let me look. I have crossed off the contact arrangements, the written follow-up, and what to prepare for future calls. The other scribble was a reminder not to let the conversation become another discussion of my old office. I think we have probably given that subject its fair share of attention. It is reassuring, in an ordinary human sense, to discover that I can talk about other things.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: We have covered a broader range than the office. There is nothing further you need to add about your household or travel plans for the administrative points we discussed. Before we move back to the formal part, would you like a moment to put the appointment notes aside and have the relevant page in front of you? There is no need to hurry through the transition.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: A moment would be useful. I have been writing in the margin and have managed to put the page I need underneath everything else. There, I have it now. I shall put the general notes to the side so I am not glancing between different subjects. This is why I prefer a clear break between a broad discussion and the formal handling of an instruction.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: We can make that break here. The correspondence questions are complete for this conversation, and I have not treated the possible contact-detail changes as amendments to your account. We are returning to the transaction part of the call now. I will leave you space to state your instruction, then use the formal wording separately.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: I want to sell from that holding, rather than add to it. The amount I am instructing for this transaction is 10k. The quantity for my instruction is 2,000 units. Please place this as a market order.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: Please confirm your final instruction: sell 2,000 units of Pioneer Balanced Opportunities Fund using a market order, with a transaction amount of 10k in American dollars. Do you authorise me to place that order?

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: Yes, I confirm that final instruction and authorise you to place the order as stated.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: Thank you. I will handle the next administrative steps through the bank's process. The formal documentation will remain separate from any covering correspondence. I will keep that covering note concise and make clear whether it contains an administrative request for you, rather than leaving you to infer that from its arrival.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: Thank you for keeping those parts distinct. I do not need to arrange another review before we finish today. I would prefer to look at my diary when the household appointments are clearer and then respond to a proposed time. In the meantime, a concise follow-up through the usual channel will suit me. I can put the rest of these notes away rather than turn them into another afternoon's work.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: We can leave the next review unscheduled today. Any future appointment proposal can give you room to suggest an alternative. If an administrative question arises when you read the correspondence, contact me through the usual route and identify the document concerned; you need not resend private material in an ordinary message. Is there anything else about the practical arrangements you wanted to raise before we finish?

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: No, that covers my list. I appreciate having had time for a proper conversation without being rushed through it. I am going to leave the study now and enjoy the garden while the weather holds. The papers can remain here for a change. Thank you for your time, Daniel Reed.

dialogue.speaker: EMPLOYEE
dialogue.text: You are welcome, Diana Clarke. Thank you for setting aside the time. I will follow up as discussed. Enjoy the rest of your afternoon. Goodbye.

dialogue.speaker: CLIENT
dialogue.text: Goodbye.
